To inspirit someone means to fill them with spirit — that is, to fill them with energy, courage, enthusiasm, or a renewed sense of purpose. When you inspirit a person or a group, you lift them from a state of low energy, doubt, or low morale into a state of aliveness, drive, and readiness to act or continue.

Think of it like this: imagine a flame that has nearly gone out. To inspirit is to breathe fresh air into that flame so it burns brightly again. The "spirit" here is not ghostly or supernatural — it refers to the inner fire that makes a person feel alive, motivated, and capable.
The Core Idea: Putting Spirit Into Someone

The key idea is a transfer of spirit. Something or someone acts as a source of energy or courage, and that energy passes into another person (or group), visibly changing how they feel and how they carry themselves.

Before being inspirited, a person might feel:

  • exhausted or burnt out
  • afraid or hesitant
  • hopeless or discouraged
  • passive and unmotivated

After being inspirited, that same person feels:

  • energized and alive
  • courageous and willing to push forward
  • hopeful and determined
  • ready to act

This shift — from low spirit to high spirit — is precisely what the word captures.

The verb "inspirit" is transitive, meaning it always acts on something. You inspirit someone or something — you don't just inspirit without an object.

Common patterns:

  • A person inspirits another person — A leader, mentor, coach, or friend lifts someone else's spirit through their words, presence, or example.
  • A thing inspirits a person — A piece of music, a great speech, a beautiful sunrise, or a meaningful event can fill a person with new energy or courage.
  • A person inspirits a group — Leaders often inspirit entire teams, armies, communities, or movements.

These examples will show you the word in action across different situations:

  1. The captain's calm confidence before the storm inspirited the entire crew.

(The captain's attitude filled the whole crew with courage and steadiness.)

  1. Her words inspirited the students who had nearly given up on their studies.

(Her words breathed new life and motivation into the students.)

  1. A single great performance can inspirit an actor who has been doubting their talent.

(A great performance can restore an actor's inner drive and confidence.)

  1. The general rode through the camp to inspirit his soldiers before dawn.

(He moved among his soldiers to fill them with courage and fighting spirit before battle.)

  1. There are rare people who simply walk into a room and inspirit everyone around them without saying a word.

(Their mere presence lifts the energy and spirit of others.)

"Inspirit" sits in the middle-to-strong range of emotional intensity. It is stronger than gently encouraging someone (which is a mild nudge) and less abrupt than galvanizing someone (which implies a sudden, almost shocking jolt into action). It most closely suggests a warm, steady, deeply felt lift — more like a tide rising than a spark exploding.

It also implies something lasting. To inspirit is not just to make someone feel good for a moment — it suggests that the spirit that has been put into them stays with them and drives them forward for some meaningful stretch of time.
Closely Related Words and How They Differ

Understanding how "inspirit" compares to similar words sharpens your understanding of what makes it unique:

  • Inspire — Very close in meaning, and often interchangeable, but "inspire" is broader. It can mean to give someone an idea, to trigger creativity, or to be the source of something great. "Inspirit" is more specifically about restoring or filling someone with inner drive, courage, and energy.
  • Encourage — Milder. It supports someone who is hesitant, giving them a gentle push. Inspiriting is a deeper, more powerful lift.
  • Hearten — Focuses specifically on giving someone hope and emotional comfort. Inspiriting is about energy and spirit broadly, not just hope.
  • Invigorate — More focused on physical freshness and energy. You might be invigorated by a cold shower. Inspiriting touches the deeper emotional and motivational level.
  • Embolden — Specifically about making someone bolder or braver, especially to do something daring. Inspiriting covers courage but also covers enthusiasm and energy more broadly.
  • Galvanize — Implies a sudden, electric shock that forces people into action, often used for groups or movements. Inspiriting is warmer and more personal.
  • Animate — Means to bring life or movement to something. Close to inspirit, but "animate" can sound more mechanical (like animating a cartoon character), while "inspirit" always carries a human emotional warmth.
Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

"Inspirit" is a formal and literary word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual conversation — almost nobody says "You really inspirited me today!" to a friend over coffee.

You will most commonly encounter it in:

  • Literature and classic texts
  • Formal speeches and writing
  • Historical accounts, especially of battles or leadership
  • Poetry and essays
  • Religious or philosophical writing

If you want to use it yourself in everyday communication, know that it will sound elevated and deliberate — which can be a good thing if you want your language to carry weight and precision.

To inspirit someone is to fill them with spirit — meaning energy, courage, enthusiasm, or a renewed will to act — lifting them from a state of low morale or weariness into one of aliveness and determination.
